title: I. Father Ferapont
paragraphs: Alyosha was woken early, before daybreak. Father Zossima had woken up feeling very weak, though he wanted to get out of bed and sit up in a chair. His mind was completely clear; his face looked tired but bright, almost joyful. It wore an expression of good humor, kindness, and warmth. "I may not live through the coming day," he told Alyosha. Then he asked to confess and take communion right away. He always confessed to Father Païssy. After taking communion, he received the rite of extreme unction. The monks gathered, and the cell gradually filled with people from the hermitage. By now it was daylight. People began arriving from the monastery. When the service ended, the elder wanted to kiss and say goodbye to everyone. Since the cell was so small, the earlier visitors stepped out to make room for others. Alyosha stood beside the elder, who had been settled back into his armchair. He talked as much as he could. His voice was weak but fairly steady.

"I've been teaching you for so many years, and talking out loud for so many years, that I've fallen into the habit of talking—so much so that it's harder for me to hold my tongue than to speak, even now, weak as I am, dear fathers and brothers," he joked, looking with emotion at the group around him.

Alyosha remembered parts of what he said afterward. Though he spoke clearly and his voice held fairly steady, his speech wandered. He touched on many things—he seemed anxious, before the moment of death, to say everything he hadn't managed to say in his life, and not simply to instruct them, but as if he were thirsting to share his joy and ecstasy with everyone and everything alive, and to open his whole heart once more before he died.

"Love one another, fathers," Father Zossima said, as far as Alyosha could recall afterward. "Love God's people. We are not holier than those outside these walls simply because we've come here and shut ourselves in—on the contrary, the very act of coming here means each of us has admitted to himself that he is worse than others, worse than everyone on earth.... And the longer a monk lives in seclusion, the more sharply he has to recognize that. Otherwise he'd have had no reason to come here at all. Only when he understands that he is not merely worse than others, but that he is answerable to everyone for everyone and for everything—for all human sins, of nations and of individuals alike—only then is the purpose of our seclusion fulfilled. Know this, dear ones: every one of us is unquestionably responsible for all people and everything on earth, not just through the general sinfulness of creation, but personally, each of us, for all mankind and every individual person. This knowledge is the crown of life for a monk, and for every human being. Monks aren't a special breed of people—they're simply what every person ought to be. Only through that knowledge does the heart soften into infinite, universal, inexhaustible love. Then every one of you will have the power to win over the whole world with love, and to wash away the world's sins with your tears.... Each of you, watch over your own heart, and confess your sins to yourself without ceasing. Don't be afraid of your sins, even once you recognize them, as long as there is repentance—but don't bargain with God. I say again: don't be proud. Be proud neither toward the small nor toward the great. Don't hate those who reject you, who insult you, who abuse and slander you. Don't hate the atheists, the teachers of evil, the materialists—and I don't just mean the good ones among them, though there are many good ones, especially nowadays—don't hate even the wicked ones. Remember them in your prayers, saying: Save, O Lord, all those who have no one to pray for them, and save too those who will not pray. And add: it is not out of pride that I offer this prayer, O Lord, for I am lower than everyone.... Love God's people, and don't let strangers lead the flock astray, for if you doze off in laziness and contemptuous pride, or worse, in greed, they will come from every direction and lead your flock away. Explain the Gospel to the people without ceasing... don't be greedy for money.... Don't love gold and silver, don't hoard it.... Have faith. Hold to the banner and raise it high."

But the elder's speech was more disjointed than Alyosha's later account of it. Sometimes he broke off entirely, as if to catch his breath and gather his strength, but he was in a kind of ecstasy. They listened with emotion, though many were puzzled by his words and found them obscure.... Afterward everyone remembered those words.

When Alyosha stepped out of the cell for a moment, he was struck by the general excitement and tension among the monks crowding around it. In some it showed as anxiety, in others as solemn devotion. Everyone was expecting some kind of marvel to happen the instant the elder died. The suspense was, in a way, almost frivolous, but even the sternest of the monks were caught up in it. Father Païssy's face looked the gravest of all.

Alyosha was quietly called away by a monk to see Rakitin, who had come from town with a strange letter for him from Madame Hohlakov. In it she told Alyosha about a strange and remarkably well-timed incident. Among the women who had come the previous day to receive Father Zossima's blessing, there had been an old woman from town, a sergeant's widow named Prokhorovna. She had asked whether she might pray for the soul of her son Vasenka, who had gone off to Irkutsk and hadn't written in over a year. Father Zossima had answered her sternly, forbidding it, saying that praying for the living as if they were dead was a kind of sorcery. Afterward he had forgiven her for her ignorance and added, "as if reading from the book of the future" (this was Madame Hohlakov's phrase), words of comfort: that her son Vasya was certainly alive, and would either come himself very soon or send a letter, and that she should go home and wait for him. "And would you believe it?" Madame Hohlakov exclaimed enthusiastically, "the prophecy has come true, literally—and more than that." The old woman had barely gotten home when they handed her a letter from Siberia that had been waiting for her. But that wasn't all: in the letter, written on the road from Yekaterinburg, Vasya told his mother he was returning to Russia with an official, and that three weeks after she received the letter he hoped "to embrace his mother."

Madame Hohlakov earnestly begged Alyosha to report this new "miracle of prophecy" to the Superior and the whole brotherhood. "Everyone, everyone ought to know of it!" she finished. The letter had been dashed off in a hurry, the writer's excitement showing in every line. But Alyosha didn't need to tell the monks—they already knew. Rakitin had instructed the monk carrying his message "to inform his reverence Father Païssy, most respectfully, that he, Rakitin, has a matter to discuss with him so pressing that he dares not put it off for even a moment, and humbly begs forgiveness for his presumption." Since the monk had delivered the message to Father Païssy before delivering it to Alyosha, Alyosha found, once he'd read the letter, that there was nothing left for him to do but hand it to Father Païssy to confirm the story.
And even that stern, cautious man, though he frowned as he read the news of the "miracle," couldn't entirely suppress some inner emotion. His eyes gleamed, and a grave, solemn smile touched his lips.
"We shall see greater things yet!" broke from him.
"We shall see greater things, greater things yet!" the monks around him repeated.

But Father Païssy, frowning again, asked everyone, at least for now, not to speak of the matter "until it is more fully confirmed, since there is so much credulity in this world, and indeed this might well have happened naturally," he added cautiously, as if to satisfy his own conscience, though he clearly didn't quite believe his own disclaimer—and his listeners could see it just as clearly.

Within the hour the "miracle" was, of course, known throughout the monastery, and to many of the visitors who had come for the mass. No one seemed more struck by it than the monk who had arrived the day before from St. Sylvester's, the small monastery of Obdorsk in the far north. He was the one who had been standing near Madame Hohlakov the day before and had earnestly asked Father Zossima, about the "healing" of the lady's daughter, "How can you presume to do such things?"

Now he was rather at a loss, unsure whom to believe. The evening before, he had visited Father Ferapont in his cell off by himself, behind the apiary, and had come away deeply impressed and awed by the visit. This Father Ferapont was the aged monk, mentioned earlier, so rigorous in fasting and keeping silence, who was hostile to Father Zossima and to the whole institution of "elders," which he regarded as a harmful and frivolous innovation. He was a formidable opponent, even though his habit of silence meant he barely spoke a word to anyone. What made him formidable was that a number of monks fully shared his feelings, and many visitors regarded him as a great saint and ascetic, even though they had no doubt he was mad. But it was precisely his madness that drew them to him.

Father Ferapont never visited the elder. Though he lived in the hermitage, no one pressed him to keep its rules, largely because he behaved as though he were mad. He was seventy-five or older, and lived in a corner beyond the apiary, in an old, decaying wooden cell that had been built long ago for another great ascetic, Father Iona, who had lived to a hundred and five, and about whose saintly doings many odd stories still circulated in the monastery and the surrounding area.

Father Ferapont had managed to get himself installed in this same isolated cell seven years earlier. It was really just a peasant's hut, though it looked like a chapel, since it held an extraordinary number of icons, with lamps burning before them perpetually—icons that people had brought to the monastery as offerings to God. Father Ferapont had been assigned to look after them and keep the lamps lit. It was said—and it was true—that he ate only two pounds of bread every three days. The beekeeper, who lived close to the apiary, brought him bread every three days, and even to this man who waited on him, Father Ferapont rarely said a word. The four pounds of bread, along with the sacramental bread the Father Superior regularly sent him after the late mass on Sundays, made up his weekly rations. The water in his jug was changed daily. He rarely appeared at mass. Visitors who came to pay him homage sometimes found him kneeling all day in prayer without so much as glancing around. If he spoke to them at all, it was brief, abrupt, strange, and almost always rude. On very rare occasions he would talk with visitors, but usually he would just utter some strange saying that was a complete riddle, and no amount of pleading could get him to explain it. He was not a priest, only a simple monk. There was a strange belief, mostly among the more ignorant, that Father Ferapont communed with heavenly spirits and would only speak with them, which was why he stayed silent with men.

The monk from Obdorsk, directed to the apiary by the beekeeper—himself a very silent and surly monk—went to the corner where Father Ferapont's cell stood. "He might talk to you, being a stranger, or you might get nothing out of him at all," the beekeeper had warned him. The monk, as he related afterward, approached in a state of considerable apprehension. It was fairly late in the evening. Father Ferapont was sitting on a low bench at the door of his cell. A huge old elm rustled softly overhead. There was an evening chill in the air. The monk from Obdorsk bowed low before the saint and asked for his blessing.
"You want me to bow to you, monk?" said Father Ferapont. "Get up!"
The monk got up.
"Blessing—be blessed! Sit beside me. Where have you come from?"

What struck the poor monk most was that, despite his strict fasting and great age, Father Ferapont still looked a vigorous old man. He was tall, stood erect, and had a thin but fresh, healthy face. There was no doubt he still had considerable strength. He was built like an athlete. Despite his great age he wasn't even fully gray, and still had thick hair and a full beard, both once black. His eyes were gray, large, and bright, but strikingly bulging. He spoke with a broad, rustic accent. He wore a peasant's long, reddish coat of coarse convict cloth, as it used to be called, with a thick rope tied round his waist. His throat and chest were bare. Under the coat, his shirt of the coarsest linen showed nearly black with dirt, not having been changed in months. People said he wore chains weighing thirty pounds under his coat. His bare feet, without stockings, were shoved into old slippers that were nearly falling apart.
"From the little Obdorsk monastery, from St. Sylvester's," the monk answered humbly, his sharp, curious, but rather frightened little eyes fixed on the hermit.
"I've stayed at your Sylvester's. I used to lodge there. Is Sylvester keeping well?"
The monk hesitated.
"You're a senseless lot! How do you keep your fasts?"

"Our diet follows the old conventual rules. During Lent there are no meals provided on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. On Tuesdays and Thursdays we have white bread, stewed fruit with honey, wild berries, or salted cabbage and wholemeal porridge. On Saturdays, white cabbage soup, noodles with peas, kasha, all with hemp oil. On weekdays we have dried fish with kasha and cabbage soup. From Monday through Saturday evening—six full days of Holy Week—nothing is cooked, and we have only bread and water, sparingly at that, and if possible we don't eat every day, just as is prescribed for the first week of Lent. On Good Friday nothing is eaten at all. Likewise on Holy Saturday we fast until three o'clock, then take a little bread and water and a single cup of wine. On Holy Thursday we drink wine and eat something cooked without oil, or nothing cooked at all, since the Council of Laodicea lays down for Holy Thursday: 'It is unseemly, by relaxing the fast on Holy Thursday, to dishonor the whole of Lent!' That's how we keep the fast. But what is that compared to you, holy father," the monk added, growing bolder, "since all year round, even at Easter, you take nothing but bread and water, and what we eat in two days lasts you a full week. It's truly marvelous—your great abstinence."
"And mushrooms?" Father Ferapont asked suddenly.
"Mushrooms?" the monk repeated, surprised.

"Yes. I can do without their bread—I don't need it at all—and go off into the forest and live there on mushrooms or berries, but they can't give up their bread here, and so they're in bondage to the devil. Nowadays the unclean claim there's no need for such fasting. Their judgment is arrogant and unclean."
"Ah, true," the monk sighed.
"And have you seen devils among them?" Ferapont asked.
"Among them? Among whom?" the monk asked timidly.

"I went to see the Father Superior last Trinity Sunday, I haven't been since. I saw a devil sitting on one man's chest, hiding under his cassock, only his horns poking out; another had one peeking out of his pocket, with such sharp eyes—he was afraid of me; another had settled in the unclean belly of one man; another was hanging round a man's neck, so that he carried him about without knowing it."
"You—can see spirits?" the monk asked.

"I tell you I can see, I can see straight through them. When I was leaving the Superior's, I saw one hiding from me behind the door—a big one, a yard and a half tall or more, with a thick, long gray tail, and the tip of his tail was caught in the crack of the door, and I was quick and slammed the door on it, pinching his tail. He squealed and started struggling, and I made the sign of the cross over him three times. And he died on the spot, like a crushed spider. He must have rotted there in the corner and be stinking by now, but they don't see it, they don't smell it. It's been a year since I've been there. I'm telling you this because you're a stranger."

"Your words are terrible! But, holy and blessed father," the monk said, growing bolder and bolder, "is it true, as people say even in distant lands, that you are in constant communication with the Holy Ghost?"
"He does fly down sometimes."
"How does he fly down? In what form?"
"As a bird."
"The Holy Ghost in the form of a dove?"
"There's the Holy Ghost and there's the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit can appear as other birds too—sometimes a swallow, sometimes a goldfinch, sometimes a blue tit."
"How do you tell him apart from an ordinary tit?"
"He speaks."
"How does he speak—in what language?"
"Human language."
"And what does he tell you?"
"Why, today he told me a fool would come to visit me and ask unseemly questions. You want to know too much, monk."
"Your words are terrible, most holy and blessed father," the monk said, shaking his head. But there was a doubtful look in his frightened little eyes.
"Do you see that tree?" Father Ferapont asked, after a pause.
"I do, blessed father."
"You think it's an elm, but to me it has another shape."
"What shape?" the monk asked, after waiting in vain for more.
"It happens at night. You see those two branches? At night it's Christ holding out His arms to me and reaching for me with them, I see it clearly and I tremble. It's terrible, terrible!"
"What's terrible about it, if it's Christ Himself?"
"Why, He'll snatch me up and carry me off."
"Alive?"
"In the spirit and glory of Elijah—haven't you heard? He'll take me in His arms and bear me away."

Though the monk went back to the cell he shared with one of the brothers in considerable confusion of mind, he still felt, at heart, a greater reverence for Father Ferapont than for Father Zossima. He was strongly in favor of fasting, and it seemed to him not at all strange that a man who kept so rigorous a fast as Father Ferapont should "see marvels." His words certainly sounded odd, but God alone could know what was hidden in those words, and weren't stranger words and deeds commonly seen among those who had sacrificed their intellects for God's glory? He was ready and eager to believe in the pinching of the devil's tail, and not only in some figurative sense. Besides, before visiting the monastery he had already held a strong prejudice against the institution of "elders," which he knew only by hearsay and believed to be a harmful innovation. He hadn't been at the monastery long before he'd picked up on the muttered complaints of some shallow brothers who disliked the practice. He was, besides, a meddlesome, nosy man who poked into everything. This was why the news of Father Zossima's fresh "miracle" left him thoroughly perplexed. Alyosha remembered afterward how their curious guest from Obdorsk had kept flitting from one group to another, listening and asking questions among the monks crowding inside and outside the elder's cell. But he hadn't paid him much attention at the time, and only remembered it later.

In fact, he had no attention to spare for it, because when Father Zossima, feeling tired again, had gone back to bed, he thought of Alyosha as he was closing his eyes, and sent for him. Alyosha ran at once. No one else was in the cell but Father Païssy, Father Iosif, and the novice Porfiry. The elder opened his weary eyes, looked intently at Alyosha, and asked him suddenly:
"Are your people expecting you, my son?"
Alyosha hesitated.
"Don't they need you? Didn't you promise someone yesterday that you'd see them today?"
"I did promise—my father—my brothers—others too."

"You see, then, you must go. Don't grieve. Rest assured I won't die without you at my side to hear my last word. That word I'll say to you, my son—it will be my last gift to you. To you, dear son, because you love me. But now go and keep your promise."

Alyosha obeyed at once, though it was hard to leave. But the promise that he would hear the elder's last word on earth, that it would be his last gift to him, Alyosha, sent a thrill of rapture through his soul. He hurried so he could finish what he had to do in town and come back quickly. Father Païssy, too, spoke some words of exhortation that moved and surprised him greatly. He spoke them as they left the cell together.

"Remember, young man, and never forget," Father Païssy began, without preamble, "that the science of this world, which has become a great power, has, especially in the last century, analyzed everything divine handed down to us in the holy books. After this ruthless analysis, the learned men of this world have nothing left of all that was once sacred. But they've only analyzed the parts and overlooked the whole, and their blindness is truly astonishing. Yet the whole still stands firm before their eyes, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Hasn't it lasted nineteen centuries? Isn't it still a living, moving power in the individual soul and in the masses of people? It remains just as strong and alive even in the souls of atheists who have torn everything else down! For even those who have renounced Christianity and attack it still, in their innermost being, follow the Christian ideal—because neither their cleverness nor the fervor of their hearts has yet managed to create a higher ideal of man and of virtue than the one Christ gave long ago. Whenever they've tried, the result has only been grotesque. Remember this above all, young man, since your dying elder is sending you out into the world. Perhaps, remembering this great day, you won't forget these words of mine, spoken from the heart to guide you, since you are young and the world's temptations are great and beyond your strength to bear. Now go, my orphan."

With these words Father Païssy blessed him. As Alyosha left the monastery and turned them over in his mind, he suddenly realized he had found a new and unexpected friend, a warmly loving teacher, in this stern monk who had always treated him so severely before. It was as though Father Zossima had bequeathed him to Father Païssy on his deathbed, and "maybe that's exactly what passed between them," Alyosha thought suddenly. The philosophical reflections he'd just heard so unexpectedly testified to the warmth of Father Païssy's heart. He was in a hurry to arm the boy's mind for the coming struggle with temptation, and to guard the young soul left in his charge with the strongest defense he could think of.
